clue.text: The apologetic bishop

parts.note: points to the cleric whose apology gives its title to a dramatic monologue by Robert Browning

explanation.surface: A bishop who keeps saying sorry.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem 'Bishop Blougram's Apology' has a worldly bishop defend his faith to a sceptical journalist; 'apologetic' means making an apology in the old sense of a reasoned defence.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's poem gives this name to a fictional churchman whose monologue is an apologia, a defence of his beliefs.

clue.text: Historian holds the belt

definitions.meaning: Henry Thomas ... wrote the History of Civilization in England
the clasp that fastens a belt; read as a verb, to fasten is to keep the belt closed

explanation.definitionFit: Henry Buckle was a Victorian historian, and the metal clasp that fastens a strap keeps it closed round the waist.

clue.text: What is this harbour seen through spectacles ?

definitions.text: What is this harbour seen through spectacles ?

indicators.note: the harbour word appears inside the two round lenses, as if seen through them

parts.note: two round lenses look like the letters O and O
a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: A puzzle question about which harbour you can see through your glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen through' reads as looking through glasses, but it puts the harbour inside the two lenses. Oporto (Porto) is a seaport in Portugal, so the whole clue also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Oporto, the Portuguese city famous for port wine, is a seaport, a harbour town.

clue.text: School book

definitions.meaning: a selective secondary school in Britain takes this name
a book setting out the rules of a language

explanation.definitionFit: A British selective secondary school is known by this word, and so is a textbook of language rules.

clue.text: Alias duennas who make biting remarks in the garden ?

definitions.text: Alias duennas who make biting remarks in the garden ?

parts.words: Alias duennas who make biting remarks in the garden
parts.note: duennas are fierce chaperones, called dragons, and biting remarks are snaps, so these are snap-dragons, garden flowers known by a Latin name

explanation.surface: Sharp-tongued chaperones gossiping in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: A duenna is an older woman chaperoning a young one, a 'dragon'; making biting remarks is snapping; snapdragons is the common name of the plants, and 'Alias' asks for their other name.
explanation.definitionFit: Snapdragons are the garden flowers whose botanical name this is, so it is another name for the same plants.

clue.text: One who takes a second to go 1,760 yards, some Cheshire cat ?

indicators.note: the runner takes on a letter, so it is joined to the front of the runner's word

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second
1,760 yards is a mile, and one who runs that distance is a miler

explanation.surface: A runner takes a second off the mile, grinning like the Cheshire Cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One who' belongs with 'go 1,760 yards' to describe a mile runner; 'takes' puts S in front of that word. The Cheshire Cat in Alice in Wonderland is famous for its grin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cheshire Cat is known for nothing so much as its broad grin, so it is a fine example of one who beams.

clue.text: I leave my decayed domicile with an air

indicators.note: a decayed house falls apart, so the letters of the home are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: the letter I is the piece that leaves the home's letters

explanation.surface: Someone abandons their crumbling home with a carefree attitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' says I goes from DOMICILE, and 'decayed' shuffles what remains, DOMCILE; 'my' is an exclamation. 'An air' is a tune, not a manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Music with an air has a tune, and tuneful music is full of melody.

clue.text: Its population was very small

parts.note: reads as a place with few inhabitants, but means one whose inhabitants were tiny, the land of six-inch people in Gulliver's Travels

explanation.surface: A remote place with hardly any residents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very small' looks like a head count but describes the people's size: in Swift's Gulliver's Travels the inhabitants of this island are six inches tall.
explanation.definitionFit: In Swift's Gulliver's Travels this island nation is peopled by tiny folk about six inches high.

clue.text: Record to make an impression

definitions.meaning: to have an effect, to sink in or be noticed

explanation.definitionFit: An official list such as a school roll is a record, and news that sinks in on someone is said to make itself felt this way.

clue.text: Very twisty torc Mary wears in Scotland

indicators.note: a torc is a twisted neck ring, and calling it very twisty tells us its letters with Mary's are wound into a new order

explanation.surface: Mary wears a twisted metal neck ring on a trip to Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: A torc is an ancient Celtic neck ornament of twisted metal, which is why 'twisty' reads so naturally. Cromarty is a town and former county in the north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromarty is a town on the Black Isle in the Scottish Highlands, so it is a place found in Scotland.

clue.text: Pipe insulation has served its time for sure !

definitions.text: Pipe insulation has served its time for sure !

parts.words: Pipe insulation has served its time for sure
parts.note: lagging round a pipe that is worn out would be old, and a convict who has served long prison terms is called by the same phrase

explanation.surface: The wrapping on the pipes is past its best and needs replacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served its time' reads as wear on the insulation, but serving time is also a prison sentence; LAG is pipe lagging, and an OLD LAG is British slang for a habitual criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-term prisoner who has done several stretches is a veteran convict, and worn-out lagging is lagging that is old.

clue.text: Out of order for such establishments to be T.T. unions, is it ?

indicators.note: something out of order is jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters as printed, T.T. being short for teetotal

explanation.surface: Asking whether teetotal trade unions would be out of order in such places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' reads as a breach of rules, but shuffles TT, UNIONS and IS IT; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Established organisations such as banks, colleges and hospitals are bodies founded and maintained for a public purpose.

clue.text: Episcopal candle-lighter

parts.note: recalls the Protestant martyr bishop who, at the stake in Oxford in 1555, said they would light such a candle in England as would never be put out

explanation.surface: A bishop's job of lighting the candles in church.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Latimer, Bishop of Worcester, was burned with Nicholas Ridley; his famous last words spoke of lighting 'such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The martyred sixteenth-century bishop is remembered for his words about lighting a candle of faith in England.

clue.text: They do the economic donkey-work

parts.note: a neddy is a British pet name for a donkey, and 'Neddy' was also the nickname of the National Economic Development Council

explanation.surface: Junior staff doing the drudgery on economic policy.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Economic Development Council of the 1960s was nicknamed Neddy (from NEDC), and its members or offshoots were neddies; neddy is also a British word for a donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Neddy is British slang for a donkey and was the nickname of the government's economic planning council, so its workers did economic labour.

clue.text: Much of its work consists of planning home production

definitions.text: Much of its work consists of planning home production

parts.words: Much of its work consists of planning home production
parts.note: the art of designing buildings spends much effort on drawing up plans for houses, read here as if it were a domestic industry

explanation.surface: A ministry whose job is planning the nation's output at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home production' sounds like domestic manufacturing in an economic plan, but it means the building of homes, which is drawn up on plans.
explanation.definitionFit: Designing buildings, especially houses, is the business of drawing up plans before construction begins.

clue.text: Is early poet of a Great Eastern Kingdom

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning, the early part of the day
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: Asking whether an early poet came from some great eastern realm.
explanation.walkthrough: Isambard Kingdom Brunel, the Victorian engineer, designed the steamship Great Eastern; 'Kingdom' is his middle name, not a realm.
explanation.definitionFit: The engineer's first name belongs to the man with the middle name Kingdom who built the Great Eastern steamship.

clue.text: Looking at one's feet

parts.note: suggests staring down at your shoes, but feet are also metrical units of verse, and examining them is analysing a poem's rhythm

explanation.surface: Someone gazing down at their shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: Feet are the units of metre in poetry; to analyse a line's metre is to scan it, and scanning also means looking over something.
explanation.definitionFit: Analysing the metrical feet of a line of verse is called by the same word as looking something over closely.

clue.text: The essence of one's alter ego ?

definitions.text: The essence of one's alter ego ?

parts.words: The essence of one's alter ego
parts.note: an alter ego is a second self, and the essence of that self would be its nature, so the phrase describes a habit so ingrained it seems inborn

explanation.surface: A question about what lies at the heart of one's other self.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alter ego' is Latin for 'other self'; the nature of a second self gives the idiom for a habit so practised that it feels instinctive.
explanation.definitionFit: An alter ego is a second self, and the idiom for an acquired habit that feels innate describes a nature that comes after the first.

clue.text: Book on anaesthetics ?

definitions.meaning: the fourth book of the Old Testament

explanation.definitionFit: The fourth book of the Bible has this title, and drugs that deaden feeling are things that numb.

clue.text: As drunk in Dunfermline

parts.note: recalls the opening of the Scottish ballad Sir Patrick Spens, where the king sits in Dunfermline town drinking the blood-red drink

explanation.surface: Someone getting drunk in a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballad 'Sir Patrick Spens' opens: 'The king sits in Dunfermline town, drinking the blude-red wine'. Dunfermline is a town in Fife, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's king drinks the blood-red drink of the grape in Dunfermline, a dark-coloured wine.

clue.text: Hop it, as the sailor's wife said to the hag

definitions.text: as the sailor's wife said to the hag
definitions.meaning: in Macbeth the witch reports that a sailor's wife told her to be gone in this archaic word

explanation.definitionFit: The archaic Shakespearean command means begone, the same as the British slang order to clear off, and the sailor's wife shouts it at the witch in Macbeth.

clue.text: Festive expansiveness

parts.note: a lavish festive meal is a large one laid out, and an expanse of space is the same word for extent

explanation.surface: Generous good cheer at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a lavish feast laid out on the table and the extent to which something stretches.
explanation.definitionFit: A lavish feast laid out on a table is a festive meal, and the word also names extent or expanse.

clue.text: The least you could call a mother who uses the second car?

parts.note: the Mini, the small British car, was the classic family second car
mum is the British everyday word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother who drives the family's second car.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mini was the small British car of the 1960s often bought as a family's second car; 'mum' is British for mother.
explanation.definitionFit: The smallest possible amount is the lowest quantity, the bare least that will do.

clue.text: Commotion left by a cutter ?

parts.note: a cutter is a fast sailing boat, and the rough water it leaves sounds like what a knife leaves, a tear

explanation.surface: Damage left behind by someone with a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is a small fast ship as well as a blade, and RIP is a tear; a tide-rip is a stretch of turbulent water where currents meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide-rip is a stretch of rough, choppy water caused by meeting currents, a commotion on the sea's surface.

clue.text: Gets up a sky-sign out of the South

indicators.note: the star sign is made to come out of, that is to surround, the letter for the South

parts.note: Aries the Ram is a sign of the zodiac, a constellation in the sky
S is the compass abbreviation for South

explanation.surface: Someone climbs to put up an illuminated sign facing south.
explanation.walkthrough: A sky-sign is an advertising sign on a rooftop, but here it is a zodiac sign; ARIES is built round S.
explanation.definitionFit: To get up and to come up from bed or a seat are the same act of rising.

clue.text: It is bound to make a man late

definitions.text: It is bound to make a man late

parts.words: It is bound to make a man late
parts.note: 'late' also means dead, as in the late Mr Smith, so the phrase describes an act that certainly leaves someone dead

explanation.surface: Something that will surely make a person behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means deceased here, not behind time; the killing of a person is certain to make them 'the late' someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing a person makes them 'the late' so-and-so, since late is the polite word for one who has died.

clue.text: Bookworm's eupepsia?

parts.note: eupepsia is good ..., and a book reader's version would be a condensed compilation of writing

explanation.surface: An avid reader with a healthy stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: Eupepsia is sound digestion; the word for digestion's verb is also a compilation or summary, a Reader's Digest kind of volume for a bookworm.
explanation.definitionFit: A compilation that condenses written works is a summary, and to process food well is the verb behind good digestion.

clue.text: Said to dare Tess

annotationWithheld.why: 'Said to dare Tess' (8): ASSERTED rearranges DARE TESS, but nothing in the clue signals the rearrangement ('to' is a link), so no honest parse names its device
